- When sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., >0.5) and forecast spikes upward, reduce the peak overshoot by 5–10% to avoid overreaction.
- If sentiment turns negative (e.g., <0.3) and forecast remains high, apply downward bias correction, especially in the first 5–7 days of the forecast horizon.
- Model tends to overestimate prices in early forecast windows (1–7 days) when sentiment is neutral or mildly positive — apply a 2–5% downward adjustment.
- In cases of sharp upward sentiment spikes, model often fails to capture mean reversion — add a 3–5 day lagged mean reversion term to dampen momentum.
- When sentiment is low or volatile (e.g., alternating ±0.1–0.3), reduce forecast volatility by smoothing the 30-day forecast with a 5-day moving average.
- If forecast consistently exceeds true outcome by >3% over 3–5 days, apply a “price ceiling” rule: cap forecast at 1.5x the 14-day moving average of historical prices.
- For sentiment history with multiple negative spikes, model tends to overcorrect — apply a “recovery buffer” rule: allow 1–2 days of upward correction after a negative sentiment dip.
